description: Allium sativum: flat leaves over a bulb of cloves.

diseases.name: Leaf Blight
diseases.pathogen: Stemphylium vesicarium (often with Alternaria porri, purple blotch)
diseases.description: A fungal blight of garlic leaves that starts on the leaf tips and on damaged tissue.
diseases.causes: Spores survive on debris and spread by wind in warm, humid weather; leaves damaged by thrips, hail or sun are infected first.
symptoms: Small yellow to tan, water-soaked spots on the leaves
Spots grow into long tan to brown lesions, often purple-edged
Leaf tips die back; lesions turn dark with spores
diseases.effect: Leaves die early, so bulbs stay small.
diseases.untreated: Severe blight cuts yield and storage quality.

steps.title: Remove blighted leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off blighted leaves when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

prevention.title: Rotate 3 years away from onions and garlic

lifecycle: Spots start on tips and wounds.
Lesions lengthen and the leaf dies back.

diseases.name: Garlic Rust
diseases.description: A rust fungus of garlic and leek leaves.
diseases.causes: Spores blow in or survive on infected allium plants; moderate temperatures with dew favour it.
symptoms: Small white flecks on the leaves
diseases.effect: Bulbs stay small and store poorly.
diseases.untreated: Severe rust can halve the yield.

steps.title: Remove badly rusted leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off badly rusted leaves when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Avoid excess nitrogen and dense planting
Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

lifecycle: Spores blow in or come from volunteers.
